questions.prompt: When does a repeated access to the same sector hit in an LRU cache?
options: When the distinct data touched since its last use is smaller than the cache
questions.explanation: That distinct data is the reuse distance; if it fits, the sector is still there.

questions.prompt: An SM has 192 KB of L1 and 1,536 resident threads. How many bytes of L1 is that per thread?
Why does a 5-tap blur's DRAM traffic stay near 'read once, write once' despite five reads per pixel in the source?
options: Neighbouring threads read overlapping data within a short window, so repeats hit in cache
questions.explanation: Short reuse distance plus neighbouring threads sharing data.

questions.prompt: A kernel sweeps cyclically over 600 KB of data many times with a 512 KB LRU cache. What hit rate do you expect after the first pass?
questions.explanation: With a cyclic sweep larger than an LRU cache, each sector is evicted just before it's needed again: the LRU cliff.

questions.prompt: Which make cache reuse more likely?
options: Processing in tiles rather than full rows or columns
Keeping the working set below cache capacity
Increasing the stride between consecutive threads
Having neighbouring threads use overlapping data
questions.explanation: Larger strides spread accesses out and hurt both coalescing and reuse.

questions.prompt: When reuse is predictable, why is shared memory often better than relying on a cache?
options: You control exactly what stays and when, with no evictions by other data
questions.explanation: Explicit management beats hoping the replacement policy keeps the right data.
